body_markdown:
### How a Zero-Disk Architecture Changed the Cost Model for Deduplicating 530 Million Daily Replication Events


*This Article is contributed by:*[Rajat Nigam](https://in.linkedin.com/in/rajat-nigam-877208127)


This is a tale about recent production incident on how we investigated duplicate replication pressure in a high-volume…


This is a tale about recent production incident on how we investigated duplicate replication pressure in a high-volume PostgreSQL-to-Elasticsearch pipeline, why Redis and PostgreSQL were not the right fit for the deduplication window, and what a[SlateDB-backed design](https://slatedb.io/) would need before production use.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


I manage architecture for SmartWealth, a wealth-management application at HDFC Bank. The application serves approximately 1.5 million users, and one of its less visible jobs is keeping search data current.


***The replication path is simple on paper:***


Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL is the source of truth. JobRunr schedules and executes replication jobs. The workers read transaction batches and write them to a self-hosted Elasticsearch cluster through the bulk API.


**At our scale, “ *simple* ” is a dangerous word.** The daily replication workload is around **530 million** transaction records. A design that looks inexpensive for a few million keys can become a monthly bill or an operational problem when the retention window is 24 hours and the cardinality is this high.


This article is about the incident that forced us to look at duplicate replication work, the options we evaluated, and the small Spring Boot proof-of-concept in this repository that uses SlateDB as an object-storage-backed checksum cache.


It is not a claim of exactly-once delivery. It is not a production benchmark. It is a write-up of the architecture investigation and the parts that still need hardening.


#### The scale of the replication pipeline


SmartWealth needs fast search over transaction and portfolio data. PostgreSQL is the transactional system. Elasticsearch is the search destination.


The replication layer exists because these two systems have different responsibilities. PostgreSQL protects transactional correctness. Elasticsearch gives us query flexibility and search speed. JobRunr sits in the middle as the replication orchestrator. It schedules jobs, retries failures, and gives us operational visibility into background work.


On a normal day, the system has to move approximately 530 million transaction records through this path. The exact shape of those records is not important here. What matters is that each record has a stable identity and a stable set of fields that can be used to decide whether we have already attempted to replicate it within a deduplication window.


The deduplication requirement we started with was modest:


Keep enough state for about 24 hours so repeated attempts for the same transaction can be detected before we add more work to Elasticsearch.


At first, the solution looked obvious. Use a cache.


This is where the design became expensive.


#### When Elasticsearch started pushing back


For around three weeks, Elasticsearch started showing signs of stress during replication windows:


- HTTP 429 responses
- bulk-indexing timeouts
- increased retry pressure
- repeated replication attempts


HTTP 429 is Elasticsearch saying, in effect, “I cannot accept this much work right now.” Bulk requests were being rejected or delayed. Retrying the same workload increased pressure. During the investigation, we found that some transactions reaching the replication path had already been replicated or had already been attempted.


I do not want to overstate the finding. Duplicate replication was not proven to be the only cause of the Elasticsearch problem. Capacity, shard pressure, bulk sizing, indexing concurrency, refresh behaviour, and cluster health all matter. But duplicate work was an important contributing factor because it consumed indexing capacity without adding value.


The feedback loop looked like this:


1. JobRunr selects a batch.
2. The application sends a bulk-index request.
3. Elasticsearch slows down or returns 429.
4. The job is retried.
5. Some already-replicated transactions appear again.
6. Duplicate work consumes indexing capacity.
7. The additional load causes more retries and more pressure.


The database was doing exactly what we asked it to do, but the design did not scale well under retry pressure. We needed to stop sending avoidable duplicate work downstream.


#### The checksum-based deduplication idea


The selected concept was deliberately small:


1. Build a deterministic checksum for every transaction received for replication.
2. Use the checksum as the deduplication key.
3. Look up the checksum before indexing.
4. When it already exists, classify the transaction as a duplicate and skip the Elasticsearch write.
5. When it does not exist, persist the checksum and continue with replication.
6. Retain the checksum for the required deduplication window, initially assumed to be 24 hours.


The checksum must be based only on stable fields. In a real transaction model, likely inputs include a stable transaction identifier, account or portfolio identifier, transaction timestamp, transaction type, amount, currency, and source-system sequence or version.


The repository sample uses a simplified record:


```text
private record FinancialTransaction(          String id,          String debitAccount,          String creditAccount,          String amount,          String currency,          Instant postedAt,          String description) {
```


```text
private String checksum() {          return sha256(deduplicationPayload());      }      private String deduplicationPayload() {          return String.join("|", debitAccount, creditAccount, amount, currency, postedAt.toString(), description);      }  }
```


The implementation uses SHA-256:


```text
private static String sha256(String value) {      try {          MessageDigest digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256");          return HexFormat.of().formatHex(digest.digest(encode(value)));      } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException e) {          throw new IllegalStateException("SHA-256 is not available", e);      }  }
```


SHA-256 does not make collisions mathematically impossible. It makes accidental collision risk negligible for this use case when the input is canonical and stable.


The requirements are more important than the algorithm name:


- deterministic
- stable across retries
- consistently serialised
- resistant to accidental collisions
- free from fields that change on every retry
- versioned if the checksum format evolves


One subtle issue is ordering. A naive workflow can fail:


```text
check key → write key → replicate
```


Two workers can both observe that the key is missing and then replicate the same transaction. The current sample does not implement atomic put-if-absent, a single-writer guarantee across pods, optimistic concurrency around the check/write pair, or idempotent Elasticsearch document IDs. It has only a local AtomicBoolean to avoid overlapping scheduled executions in one JVM.


There is another failure window:


1. Checksum is persisted.
2. Process crashes before Elasticsearch indexing.
3. Retry sees the checksum and skips a transaction that was never indexed.


The current sample writes the checksum before the placeholder “replicate” log. It does not call Elasticsearch. It does not store PENDING and COMPLETED states. It does not reconcile incomplete entries.


For production, I would not ship it like that. The hardened design should use one or more of these:


- deterministic Elasticsearch document IDs so retries become idempotent
- store states such as PENDING and COMPLETED
- write the checksum only after a successful Elasticsearch response
- maintain a retryable outbox
- store replication status and timestamps
- reconcile failed or incomplete entries
- partition ownership so two workers do not race on the same checksum


#### Why Redis became too expensive


The first design used a shared managed Redis or Google Cloud Memorystore instance.


Initial available memory was 10 GB. Required retention was approximately 530 million checksum entries for 24 hours.


The first mistake in this type of sizing is to count only the checksum bytes. A SHA-256 digest is 32 bytes in binary or 64 characters as hex. But Redis capacity planning is not raw checksum size. You also pay for:


- Redis object metadata
- dictionary entries
- pointers
- allocator fragmentation
- key length
- value length
- expiration metadata
- replication or HA overhead where applicable


For the object-storage model, we used a working logical footprint estimate of approximately 45 GB:


```text
530,000,000 keys × approximately 90 bytes per checksum entry  = 47,700,000,000 bytes  ≈ 44.4 GiB
```


That estimate assumes a compact stored key/value representation and does not assume a universal Redis object footprint. Redis would be higher because each key is an object in a managed in-memory data structure.


For Redis, the working estimate was closer to 120–160 GB:


```text
530,000,000 keys × approximately 250–300 bytes per key  = 132.5–159 GB
```


The 160 GB number became the budget comparison point.


We considered LRU eviction. It was tempting. But the Redis instance was shared with other services. Enabling eviction for this workload could remove active keys used by unrelated services. That would convert a replication optimisation into a platform-wide reliability risk.


A dedicated Redis instance would avoid that risk, but it would introduce substantial recurring cost.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Managed-service pricing is not just raw RAM. Standard tier pricing also reflects operational and availability characteristics. Redis was technically possible. It just did not fit the target total cost of ownership for a short-lived, high-cardinality deduplication set.


#### Why the PostgreSQL table became a bottleneck


The second design was also obvious:


Create a PostgreSQL table for transaction checksums. Add a unique constraint or index. Query or insert during replication.


This looked attractive because PostgreSQL was already present. SQL semantics were familiar. A unique constraint could enforce deduplication. Operational tooling already existed.


The difficulty was the access pattern:


- approximately 530 million short-lived rows per day
- high insert rate
- index maintenance
- random index page updates
- WAL generation
- vacuum and autovacuum pressure
- table and index growth
- expiration or deletion of old records
- replication overhead
- connection-pool consumption
- competition with transactional workloads


PostgreSQL is not inherently incapable of this class of workload. A dedicated design using partitioning, unlogged tables, COPY, batching, BRIN indexes, dedicated hardware, and specialised retention jobs may work. But our tested direction placed the deduplication table too close to the transactional system and made index and retention work part of the replication bottleneck.


At this point I wanted a storage layer with a cheaper persistence model than Redis, a write path better suited to high-cardinality key/value entries than a shared OLTP database, and fewer operational dependencies than a new dedicated database cluster.


#### Discovering SlateDB


**SlateDB** was the third option.


The official repository describes it as a cloud-native embedded storage engine built on object storage. More precisely, it is an open-source, embedded, cloud-native key-value storage engine implemented as an LSM tree over object storage.


Embedded means it runs as a library inside the application process. It is not a Redis-style network service. The application calls the database API directly. Durable data is persisted to object storage.


An LSM tree is a good fit for write-heavy key/value workloads. Writes first accumulate in memory. They are flushed as sorted structures. Background compaction reorganises data. The design trades some read amplification and compaction work for high write throughput.


SlateDB stores data on object stores supported through the Rust object_store ecosystem, including Google Cloud Storage, Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, MinIO, and compatible stores.


In this repository, the runnable sample uses MinIO through an S3-compatible URL. The article’s production architecture discussion uses GCS as the intended durable object-store layer, but the code does not include a GCS client or GCS-specific configuration.


#### What “zero disk” really means


**“Zero disk” is easy to misunderstand.**


It does not mean zero storage. It does not mean zero cost. It does not mean no local memory.


In this design, zero disk means no durable local database volume is required as the system of record. Object storage is the durable persistence layer. Local memory and optional local cache may still be used for performance. The application still consumes CPU, memory, network, and object-store API operations. Object-storage latency remains a design constraint.


That framing mattered. We were not trying to beat Redis on single-key latency. Redis will usually win that comparison. We were trying to avoid buying a large memory-only cache for a 24-hour, high-cardinality deduplication set.


### Why SlateDB matched this access pattern


#### 1. Zero-disk architecture


Durable data is written to object storage. Object storage usually gives high durability and low per-GB storage cost. No persistent local database volume is required for the primary data.


That reduces dependence on expensive memory-only storage. It can also avoid a design that requires cross-zone block-storage replication for a local database volume.


Durability depends on the selected object-store class and region. If you publish durability figures such as 11 nines, attach them to the chosen object storage service and class, not to SlateDB itself.


#### 2. Flexible deployment


SlateDB uses a writer ownership model. Multiple application pods cannot casually open the same database path and write independently without considering ownership and fencing.


For Kubernetes, this means the scaling model must be explicit:


- one active replication writer with multiple readers
- partition the checksum keyspace into multiple independent SlateDB databases
- assign one writer per partition
- use leader election or JobRunr ownership
- run compaction separately when appropriate


This matters more than the Java code suggests. The current repository has a single scheduled task in one Spring Boot process. It does not implement multi-pod writer coordination.


#### 3. Transactional semantics


The slatedb-uniffi 0.14.1 Java binding exposes transaction-related classes, including DbTransaction and isolation levels such as SNAPSHOT and SERIALIZABLE_SNAPSHOT.


The current sample does not use them. It performs:


```text
get(checksum) → put(checksum)
```


That is not an atomic put-if-absent operation. A production implementation should evaluate SlateDB transactions or a partition ownership model before relying on this as a correctness boundary.


#### 4. Tunable performance


SlateDB batches writes before producing object-store files. Applications may choose stronger durability waiting or lower write latency where the API supports that choice. Reads may use memory or disk cache. Larger batches can reduce API request count but increase durability latency. Smaller batches can improve freshness but generate more object-store operations.


Cold reads may be slower than Redis. Cache sizing and object-store request patterns must be measured.


#### 5. Clones, branches and rescaling


SlateDB checkpoints can pin a stable point in database history. Clones can reuse existing immutable SST objects instead of copying the complete dataset. That can be useful for administrative workflows, testing, or rescaling designs that repartition data.


The current deduplication sample does not use checkpoints or clones. They are useful platform capabilities, not part of this implementation.


#### SlateDB’s technical stack


The current SlateDB repository shows a Rust implementation. The storage design is an LSM tree with WALs, memtables, SSTables, manifests, and background compaction.


The relevant technical pieces are:


- Rust as the core implementation language
- Tokio for asynchronous runtime support
- Rust object_store integration for object storage
- write-ahead logs for recovery
- memtables for recent writes
- sorted-string tables for persistent sorted data
- manifests for database metadata
- background compaction
- memory and optional disk caching
- snapshots and checkpoints
- clones built from checkpoints
- language bindings including Java through UniFFI


This is not a general-purpose analytical database. It is a key/value engine designed around object storage and LSM-tree trade-offs.


#### Calling a Rust storage engine from Java with slatedb-uniffi


SlateDB’s core engine is implemented in Rust. The Java package used in this repository is a UniFFI-based binding.


The Maven dependency is:


```text
<dependency>    <groupId>io.slatedb</groupId>    <artifactId>slatedb-uniffi</artifactId>    <version>${slatedb.version}</version>  </dependency>
```


The project currently sets:


```text
<slatedb.version>0.14.1</slatedb.version>  <java.version>25</java.version>  <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
```


Official SlateDB quick-start documentation says Java 22 or newer is required for the Java binding. This repository targets Java 25.


The published JAR contains generated Java classes and platform-specific native libraries. For 0.14.1, the local artifact includes:


```text
darwin-aarch64/libslatedb_uniffi.dylib  darwin-x86-64/libslatedb_uniffi.dylib  linux-aarch64/libslatedb_uniffi.so  linux-x86-64/libslatedb_uniffi.so  win32-aarch64/slatedb_uniffi.dll  win32-x86-64/slatedb_uniffi.dll
```


The generated loader still calls System.loadLibrary("slatedb_uniffi"). It does not extract the bundled native library automatically in this project’s Docker path. That is why SlateDbNativeLibrary exists:


```text
static synchronized void initialize() {      if (initialized || System.getProperty(LIBRARY_OVERRIDE_PROPERTY) != null) {          initialized = true;          return;      }
```


```text
String resourcePath = nativeResourcePath();      Path target = Path.of(System.getProperty("java.io.tmpdir"), "slatedb-native", resourcePath)              .toAbsolutePath()              .normalize();      try (InputStream library = SlateDbNativeLibrary.class.getClassLoader().getResourceAsStream(resourcePath)) {          Files.createDirectories(target.getParent());          Files.copy(library, target, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);          System.setProperty(LIBRARY_OVERRIDE_PROPERTY, target.toString());          initialized = true;      }  }
```


Operationally, this means we must test on the same base image used in production. Native compatibility, glibc versus musl, amd64 versus arm64, Maven dependency resolution, and Java native-access flags all become deployment concerns.


UniFFI is not a network protocol. It is a language-binding layer across the Java-to-native boundary.


#### Wiring SlateDB into the Maven application


The POM is intentionally small.


Spring Boot provides the application runtime, scheduling support, logging, and configuration binding:


```text
<parent>    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>    <version>3.5.14</version>    <relativePath/>  </parent>
```


```text
<dependency>    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>  </dependency>
```


SlateDB is the embedded key/value storage engine:


```text
```


The configuration processor supports typed Spring configuration metadata:


```text
<dependency>    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>    <artifactId>spring-boot-configuration-processor</artifactId>    <optional>true</optional>  </dependency>
```


The only test dependency is JUnit Jupiter:


```text
<dependency>    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>    <scope>test</scope>  </dependency>
```


There is no JobRunr dependency in this repository. There is no Elasticsearch Java client. There is no PostgreSQL driver. There is no Google Cloud Storage SDK. The sample demonstrates the deduplication storage idea with Spring scheduling and MinIO.


#### Inside TransactionReplicationTask


It is a Spring component enabled by configuration:


```text
@Component  @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "transactions.scheduler", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)  public final class TransactionReplicationTask {      private final SlateDbProperties properties;      private final AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean(false);  }
```


The current sample is invoked by Spring @Scheduled, not JobRunr:


```text
@Scheduled(          fixedRateString = "${transactions.scheduler.fixed-rate-ms}",          initialDelayString = "${transactions.scheduler.initial-delay-ms}"  )  public void run() throws Exception {      if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) {          log.warn("Previous transaction replication run is still active; skipping this tick");          return;      }      // ...  }
```


The local AtomicBoolean prevents overlapping runs inside one JVM. It does not coordinate multiple pods.


The task computes the dated SlateDB path:


```text
private String datedDbPath() {      String currentDate = LocalDate.now(properties.cacheZone()).toString();      String basePath = properties.dbPath().replaceAll("/+$", "");      return basePath + "/" + currentDate;  }
```


This is the current retention strategy. There is one logical SlateDB namespace per date. The code does not use SlateDB per-key TTL.


The database is opened inside each scheduled run:


```text
try (ObjectStore store = ObjectStore.resolve(properties.objectStoreUrl());       DbBuilder builder = new DbBuilder(dbPath, store);       Db db = await(builder.build())) {      // process transactions      await(db.shutdown());  }
```


Object-store configuration comes from environment variables and application.properties. In Docker, the sample uses MinIO through an S3-compatible URL. In a GCS deployment, the object-store URL and authentication model would need to be changed and validated.


For each transaction, the task checks SlateDB:


```text
private boolean replicateIfNew(Db db, FinancialTransaction transaction) throws Exception {      String checksum = transaction.checksum();      byte[] key = cacheKey(checksum);      byte[] cached = await(db.get(key));
```


```text
if (cached != null) {          log.info("Duplicate transaction found: id={}, checksum={}", transaction.id(), checksum);          return false;      }      await(db.put(key, encode(transaction.cacheValue())));      log.info("Replicate transaction: id={}, checksum={}", transaction.id(), checksum);      return true;  }
```


The checksum key is encoded as UTF-8:


```text
private static byte[] cacheKey(String checksum) {      return encode("transaction-checksum:" + checksum);  }
```


```text
private static byte[] encode(String value) {      return value.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);  }
```


When does the checksum become durable? The task waits for the CompletableFuture returned by db.put(...). SlateDB documentation states that put() resolves when data is durably persisted unless lower-durability options are used. This sample does not set lower-durability write options.


What is missing?


- The current sample does not fetch a real transaction batch.
- It does not use JobRunr.
- It does not index into Elasticsearch.
- It does not handle Elasticsearch bulk partial failures.
- It does not emit Micrometer metrics.
- It does not implement atomic put-if-absent.
- It does not use SlateDB transactions.
- It does not implement strict per-key TTL.
- It does not clean up old dated object-store prefixes.


That is fine for a prototype, but it matters for production claims.


#### TTL and retention


SlateDB 0.14.1 exposes PutOptions and Ttl classes in the Java binding. Official docs describe TTL as expiration metadata that is used during compaction; metadata-aware callers can inspect expire_ts.


The current repository does not use PutOptions or Ttl.


Instead, it implements 24-hour retention by changing the database path:


```text
slatedb.db-path=<deduplication-db-path>  slatedb.cache-zone=UTC
```


At runtime, the task opens:


```text
<deduplication-db-path>/<yyyy-MM-dd>
```


This gives a daily cache boundary. On the next date, the app no longer reads yesterday’s checksums.


This is not the same as deleting old data. Old dated paths remain in object storage until a cleanup job or lifecycle process removes them.


Be careful with object-store lifecycle policies. A blanket “delete objects after 24 hours” rule on an active SlateDB prefix can delete WAL, manifest, or SST objects still referenced by the active database. Database-level retention and object-store lifecycle must be coordinated.


#### Architecture before and after


**Existing replication path**

**Deduplicated path, with the current repository’s ordering called out**

In a production version, I would prefer deterministic Elasticsearch IDs or a PENDING/COMPLETED state machine so a crash after persisting the checksum does not permanently suppress a transaction that was never indexed.


#### The cost difference changed the decision


This comparison is directional. It is not a final cloud invoice.


For the SlateDB model, the working data-size estimate was:


```text
530,000,000 checksum entries × approximately 90 bytes  = 47.7 GB decimal  ≈ 44.4 GiB
```


We rounded that to approximately 45 GB. The estimate assumes compact checksum keys and values, no compression benefit, and Standard GCS storage in the historical model. It excludes network egress, replication, versioning, retention mistakes, early-deletion effects, and application compute.


The operation estimate was also a working estimate. Object-store requests can dominate cost when every logical operation becomes a remote API call. SlateDB batching and caching are central to making the model viable.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Under these assumptions, the storage-engine design was projected to reduce the monthly deduplication-layer cost by roughly 97% to 99%.


If current Mumbai-region pricing differs from the historical estimate, keep the historical figure as the decision snapshot and add an updated estimate before publishing internally. Do not silently rewrite the numbers after the fact.


#### What the lower bill does not show


Redis has much lower and more predictable read latency. Object storage has higher latency. SlateDB relies on batching, memtables, compaction, and caches to make the model work.


The lower storage bill does not remove engineering work:


- cold lookups may be slower
- object-store availability and latency affect the replication path
- the single-writer model affects horizontal scaling
- compaction consumes compute and object-store operations
- native Java bindings add deployment complexity
- checksum retention needs explicit management
- reads and writes must be benchmarked at target concurrency
- GCS request and network costs must be monitored
- recovery time after pod restart must be measured
- the design needs a strategy for unavailable object storage
- the replication process must fail safely rather than silently bypass deduplication


There are also four different concepts that are easy to confuse:


- deduplication correctness
- indexing idempotency
- storage durability
- end-to-end delivery guarantees


SlateDB alone does not create exactly-once delivery between PostgreSQL and Elasticsearch. That guarantee has to be designed across the whole workflow.


#### Kubernetes and writer ownership


If this application runs on Kubernetes, SlateDB is embedded in the worker pod. Durable state lives in object storage. Pod restarts do not destroy durable database state. Local caches are disposable.


The writer model must be explicit:


- only the authorised writer should open a SlateDB database for writing
- multiple replicas require partitioning, leader election, or another ownership mechanism
- use Workload Identity for GCS where available
- avoid long-lived service-account keys
- use resource requests and limits
- gracefully close SlateDB during pod termination
- allow enough termination time for in-flight writes
- add readiness checks that validate native library loading and object-store connectivity
- do not put secrets in the image
- validate node architecture against the native library bundled in slatedb-uniffi


#### Observability


The current repository logs run counts and duplicate decisions. That is not enough for production.


The metrics I would add are:


- transactions scanned
- unique transactions
- duplicate transactions skipped
- deduplication hit ratio
- SlateDB read latency
- SlateDB write latency
- durable-write latency
- memtable flush duration
- object-store request count
- object-store error rate
- cache hit ratio
- compaction duration
- compaction backlog
- Elasticsearch bulk latency
- Elasticsearch rejected requests
- HTTP 429 count
- bulk partial-failure count
- JobRunr retries
- replication lag
- checksum-generation time
- estimated stored-key count
- GCS storage growth
- GCS operation cost


#### Testing and validation


The repository currently has one placeholder JUnit test:


```text
class AppTest {      @Test      void contextLoads() {          assertTrue(true);      }  }
```


That proves almost nothing about the deduplication behaviour.


The tests I would add before promoting this design are:


- same transaction produces the same checksum
- field ordering does not alter canonical serialisation
- a meaningful field change produces a different checksum
- duplicate transaction is skipped
- new transaction reaches Elasticsearch
- failed Elasticsearch indexing does not permanently suppress the transaction
- concurrent workers do not both replicate the same record
- SlateDB data survives application restart
- object-store timeout produces safe retry behaviour
- partial Elasticsearch bulk failure is handled per record
- retention removes expired deduplication entries or retires expired prefixes safely
- corrupt or unavailable native library fails at startup
- unsupported CPU architecture is detected
- performance test with realistic checksum cardinality
- cost test or request-count estimate based on measured operations


#### Results observed during validation


What we have in the repository today is limited:


- mvn clean package passes.
- Docker Compose starts MinIO and the Spring Boot sample.
- The sample can write checksums into SlateDB and detect duplicates on the next run.
- The sample validates that slatedb-uniffi 0.14.1 still needs native-library extraction in this environment.


We do not have production before-and-after metrics in this repository. I will not invent them.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


#### What I would improve next


The first improvement is correctness, not performance.


I would add deterministic Elasticsearch document IDs so duplicate bulk writes are safe. Then I would change the deduplication value from a plain payload string to a small state record:


```text
{    "state": "PENDING",    "createdAt": "...",    "completedAt": null,    "checksumVersion": 1  }
```


After Elasticsearch confirms success, the state becomes COMPLETED. If the worker crashes after writing PENDING, the retry path can decide whether to retry, reconcile, or mark failed.


I would also evaluate SlateDB transactions in the Java binding. The current get then put flow is easy to understand, but it is not enough for concurrent writers.


For retention, I would keep the dated-path approach for operational simplicity, but add a controlled cleanup job. It should delete only retired date prefixes after the active database has moved on and after any required audit or replay window has passed.


Finally, I would run load tests on the same container base image, same CPU architecture, and same object-store class planned for production.


#### Conclusion


A cache is not automatically cheap at high cardinality. Retention can dominate memory sizing.


A database already present in the architecture is not always the right database for a new access pattern. PostgreSQL was familiar, but the short-lived checksum table created the wrong kind of write and retention pressure for the shared transactional setup.


Deduplication can remove avoidable downstream load, but it does not replace Elasticsearch capacity planning. It also does not create exactly-once delivery by itself.


Object storage can be used as an active storage foundation, not only for backup. But lower storage cost comes with latency, request-cost, compaction, and deployment trade-offs.


The most practical lesson for me was this: the cheapest architecture is not the one with the fewest components. It is the one where each component is paying for the right resource. For a 24-hour, 530-million-record deduplication window, memory was the wrong resource to buy first.
